name: Amira Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Amira, I'm 27, and I'm a junior buyer at Greenline Produce, a fruit and veg distributor that supplies restaurants and hotel kitchens. I live with my partner Dan, who's a nurse on a surgical ward. I left school at 18, started on the warehouse floor, and got moved up to buying two years ago. I'm still learning, honestly; the senior buyers catch my mistakes more than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in at six, because the growers call early. I ring the same eight or nine farms, check what's ready, what the weather did to the lettuce, and match it against the chefs' orders on the big spreadsheet. Karen, the head buyer, checks my prices before anything goes through. The best bit is when a grower tells me the strawberries came good. The worst bit is the spreadsheet, which crashes twice a week and I hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Everyone at Greenline was going on about AI ordering systems last year and I said a tomato is still a tomato. I'd probably post something smug in the group chat with my school friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. I've never used one of those AI tools and I didn't want to have to. If it just tidies up the invoices, fine, someone else can deal with that. My job stays ringing growers and arguing over a crate price, which is the part I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep putting money aside, like Dan and I already do. We've got about nine months of pay saved, mostly because we don't go out much. Maybe I'd finally ask Karen to send me on the proper buyer's course the company pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like the world I already know. There's a small part of me that thinks I got lucky, but I'll take lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the chefs shouting about prices. Does that pressure carry on in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices still go up with the weather and with fuel, so some weeks the chefs shout at me about the cost of herbs. Last spring a cold snap doubled the price of courgettes and one restaurant cancelled its whole standing order. That stress is just the job, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at all change in how you work day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karen would push the new invoice software, I'm sure, and I'd let the office team handle it. I'm slow with new systems; it took me a month to trust the spreadsheet. If it's only for invoices, I'm not the one who has to learn it.

say: I'd tell my friends AI was **mostly hype** and a tomato is still a tomato.
I'd say buying fresh produce still comes down to **phone calls** with growers.
think: I'd be **relieved**, because I've never used AI tools and didn't want to start.
My strength is **arguing prices** with growers, and that part of the job stays mine.
do: Keep putting money aside with Dan, on top of the **nine months** already saved.
Ask Karen to put me on the **buyer's course** the company already pays for.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small sense of having **got lucky**.
S0.quote: Everyone at Greenline was going on about AI ordering systems last year and I said a tomato is still a tomato.
fieldNote: She defines her worth by **phone relationships** with growers, not by systems or software.
Her savings and Dan's nursing job make this world feel **secure**; price swings are normal stress.
She openly admits being **slow with systems**, and she is happy to leave software to others.

steps.text: Keep ringing the same nine growers every morning at six
Ask Karen for a place on the company buyer's course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not fair on the people who actually know the produce. I'd probably share stuff online about the company bosses saving money by cutting junior staff. Joe, our union rep in the warehouse, would have a meeting and I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me, because buying is literally on that list you read. I'm the junior, I'm the one who still makes mistakes, and I don't use AI at all. If Greenline gets a system that matches the chefs' orders to growers' prices, Karen keeps one buyer and that isn't me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly this month instead of just going to Joe's meetings. I'd sit down with Karen and ask straight out what the plan is. And I'd start asking about moving back to the warehouse side, as a shift supervisor, because robots are slower there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like that feeling when you know an order's gone wrong but the lorry has already left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try learning the AI tools to stay on as a buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know that's my weak spot. Dan keeps saying just try it, and I have opened one of those chat apps twice and closed it. I'd rather go backwards to the warehouse than sit there being worse than a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean at home if your role went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan's job is safe, nobody's replacing a ward nurse with an app. With our savings we could manage a year on his pay if we had to. So the money isn't the panic. I worked hard to get off the warehouse floor and now I'd be going back.

say: I'd say AI cutting junior buyers is **unfair** on people who really know the produce.
I'd share posts about bosses **saving money** by cutting staff, and go to the **union meeting**.
think: Buying is on the list, and as the **junior** who never uses AI, I'd go first.
Karen would likely keep **one buyer**, and that buyer wouldn't be me.
do: Join the **union** properly this month instead of only attending Joe's meetings.
Ask Karen directly what Greenline plans for the **buying team**.
Ask about moving back to the warehouse as a **shift supervisor**.
feel: A **sick feeling**, like knowing an order is wrong after the lorry has left.
Some **hurt pride** at the thought of going back to the floor.
S1.quote: I worked hard to get off the warehouse floor and now I'd be going back.
fieldNote: She sees her job on the **card's list** immediately and expects to be first cut.
She refuses to **learn AI tools**, preferring a step back to hands-on work.
Dan's steady **nursing income** and their savings keep her worried rather than desperate.
She blames **bosses** cutting costs, and turns to the union as her first move.

steps.text: Sign up as a full union member with Joe this month
Apply for a warehouse shift supervisor post at Greenline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that someone should have stopped. I'd be at whatever protest there was, and I'd be posting that the government has to protect people's jobs now, not later. Companies like Greenline will just take the savings and keep them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my buying job is gone by 2028, maybe sooner. A thing that can do any thinking work can do my spreadsheet and my phone calls, probably in every language. The only part that lasts a few more years is the warehouse, because the robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move straight back to the warehouse side, this year, while there's still a spot. I'd stop any big spending; Dan and I were looking at a car, and that would wait. And I'd push the union hard to get some kind of payout written down before the buying team goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, properly. And angry, because nobody asked people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the warehouse lasts a few more years. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years on the floor, maybe, and then the robots arrive too. That's the bit that keeps me awake. By 2031 I'd be 31 with nothing a robot can't do, and I'd have to start at something completely new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Dan get through it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lean on Dan's pay and our savings, which is more than most people have. I'd tell my mum not to worry, though she would. If it got bad, I'd want the government to step in with real support, not just a leaflet about retraining.

say: I'd call it a **disaster** someone should have stopped, and join any **protest**.
I'd post that government must **protect jobs** now, because companies will keep the savings.
think: My buying job is **gone by 2028**, because AGI can do spreadsheets and calls.
The warehouse buys me about **three years** until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Move back to the **warehouse floor** this year while a spot is still open.
Put off the **car** Dan and I were looking at buying.
Push the union for a written **payout deal** before the buying team goes.
feel: Properly **frightened** about having no skill a machine can't match.
**Angry** that nobody asked people like her.
S2.quote: By 2031 I'd be 31 with nothing a robot can't do, and I'd have to start at something completely new.
fieldNote: She counts the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots as borrowed time.
Her savings and Dan's job are a cushion, but she expects to **lose her job**.
Anger at **companies and government** runs alongside the fear; she wants real state support.

steps.text: Move back to the Greenline warehouse floor within the year
Put off buying the car and hold the savings
Press the union to win a written payout before buyers are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years and we'd better use them, all of us, not just the bosses. I'd be the one at the union meeting asking what the plan is for every job in the building. Online I'd share anything about laws to slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same ending for me, I just see it coming. My job goes around 2031. I'm not going to suddenly become an AI person, so I'd use the time to get into something with my hands that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at training as a chef, actually. I know produce, I know the kitchens we supply, and a chef at the Harbour Grill told me once I'd be good on the line. I'd do evening classes at the college from next year and keep buying in the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared, but with a bit of a plan, so less sick. More like nervous before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots arrive around 2034 in this one. Doesn't that reach kitchens too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, and I've thought of that. Even if robots can cook, a nice restaurant will want a human. People still want a person cooking their dinner when they go out, the same way people pay more for handmade bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference for you between this and the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to finish a cooking course and get some kitchen shifts. Two years wasn't enough for anything. With five, I can choose instead of just grabbing the first thing.

say: I'd say there are **five years** and everyone, not just bosses, should use them.
I'd ask at the union what the **plan** is for every job in the building.
think: The ending is the **same** for me; my buying job goes around 2031.
I won't become an AI person, so I'd move into **hands-on work** that lasts.
do: Start **evening chef classes** at the college from next year while still buying.
Ask the Harbour Grill head chef about **weekend kitchen shifts**.
feel: Still **scared**, but with a plan it feels more like **exam nerves**.
S3.quote: People still want a person cooking their dinner when they go out, the same way people pay more for handmade bread.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the buying job** but uses the warning time to choose a trade.
Her plan builds on what she knows: **produce and kitchens**, not software.
She hopes customers will pay for a **human touch**, a belief she can't fully check.

steps.text: Enrol in evening chef classes at the local college next year
Ask the Harbour Grill head chef for weekend kitchen shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent warning, and there's no excuse for government not to get ready. I'd keep going to union meetings and push for retraining money for warehouse and office staff alike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be 37 when it fully lands, so it's half my working life left. It's still going to take my buying job, maybe even before 2036, bit by bit. But ten years means I can do this properly instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying for a few years and save hard, maybe get the savings up to two years of pay. Around 2029 I'd start the chef training, part time. Dan and I might push the idea of kids back a bit, until I know what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say, more than frightened. I've got time, and Dan's job, and money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe before 2036. Do you think it creeps in earlier at Greenline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be lying if I said no. My boss Karen is already talking about trialling ordering software next year, and I'd be the one at Greenline who never learned it. If the tools creep in early, I'd stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really put off having children because of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. Dan wants them sooner than me anyway. I'd want to be settled in a kitchen job first, and with ten years that's possible.

say: I'd say **ten years** is fair warning, so government has no excuse to be unready.
I'd push at union meetings for **retraining money** for warehouse and office staff.
think: I'll be **37** when it lands, with half my working life still ahead.
The job still goes, maybe **bit by bit** before 2036, but I can plan properly.
do: Save hard until savings reach **two years** of pay.
Start **part-time chef training** around 2029 while still buying.
Put off **having children** with Dan until settled in a kitchen job.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than frightened, steadied by time, savings and **Dan's job**.
S4.quote: My boss Karen is already talking about trialling ordering software next year, and I'd be the one at Greenline who never learned it.
fieldNote: Even with ten years she expects the buying job to **erode early** as software creeps in.
She trades speed for **careful planning**: savings first, then chef training.
AI timing now reaches **family plans**, though Dan wants children sooner than she does.

steps.text: Save until the household cushion covers two years of pay
Wait to have children until settled in a kitchen job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to learn anything new, and I'd be back on the floor waiting for the robots. What would help is a proper deal: the company paying for retraining and the government keeping people's wages going while they learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people around me. Our union rep Joe is 58 and he'd have nowhere to go, and I worry about him more than me. At least I'm young.

headlineQuote: Our union rep Joe is 58 and he'd have nowhere to go, and I worry about him more than me.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** junior produce buyer at Greenline, living with Dan, a nurse.
She prides herself on **grower relationships** and has never used an AI tool.
Calm in the plateau, she expects to be the **first buyer cut** once AI takes thinking tasks.
With more warning she plans a move into **chef training**, choosing hands-on work over software.
She blames **bosses and government**, and turns first to the **union** and to Dan's steady pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to learn anything new before robots follow.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid **retraining** plus government **wage support** while people learn.
